blocks.heading: How the Moratorium Period Actually Works

items.text: The moratorium period is the window during your course, plus a grace period after it ends, when you are not required to repay the loan's principal.
Some lenders, including Prodigy Finance, require no payment at all, neither principal nor interest, during the course and a grace period of around six months after it ends.

Other lenders, including MPOWER Financing and many Indian banks and NBFCs, require simple interest payments during the study period itself, with principal repayment starting only after the grace period ends.

blocks.heading: Do Not Fund the Degree Alone

items.text: A large education loan is only a good decision if it is genuinely funding a stronger earning outcome, and that outcome is never guaranteed the day you land.

Check your specific program's recent placement data, typical starting salary range, and how that number is described, median, strong outcome, or a small number of exceptional cases, rather than relying on a single headline salary figure from a university brochure or agent.

Build a second, more portable skill alongside your main degree, and keep your professional network and job search active in both your target country and India, so a slow visa or hiring market in one place does not leave you with no income and a full moratorium clock running out.

blocks.heading: Education Loans for Study Abroad in India
supporting: Yes. Public-sector banks offer limited collateral-free loans, usually capped around Rs 40-50 lakh, only for applicants admitted to specific premier institutions on the bank's approved list. NBFCs such as Avanse and HDFC Credila offer larger unsecured loans, sometimes beyond Rs 75 lakh to over Rs 1 crore, for students admitted to a wider set of recognised universities, based on the co-applicant's income and the course's employability. International lenders like Prodigy Finance and MPOWER Financing lend without any collateral or Indian co-signer at all, underwriting the loan mainly on your admitted program and projected future income.

Take a secured loan if your family can offer property, fixed deposits, or another acceptable asset as collateral and does not mind the paperwork and valuation time, it typically comes with a lower interest rate and a higher loan ceiling. Take an unsecured loan if you have no collateral to offer, need faster sanction, or are targeting a university that qualifies for a public-sector bank's collateral-free list. The trade-off is a rate that usually runs 1-2 percentage points higher and a lower maximum loan amount at most lenders.
